concepts.title: Caste in the Past: Varna, Jati and the Defining Features
concepts.section: 3.1 Caste and the Caste System - Caste in the Past
concepts.definition: Caste is an institution tied to the Indian subcontinent, known in Indian languages through two words: varna, a four-fold all-India division into brahmana, kshatriya, vaishya and shudra (with the excluded panchamas), and jati, the regional sub-classification of hundreds of castes and sub-castes. Its defining features are that caste is fixed by birth, marriage is endogamous within the group, food and food-sharing rules apply, castes sit in a hierarchy of rank, sub-castes create segmental organisation, and occupations were hereditary.
concepts.formula: caste_terms = varna (four_fold_all_india) + jati (regional_subcastes) ; features = birth + endogamy + food_rules + hierarchy + segmental + hereditary_occupation
concepts.key_idea: The early Vedic varna order of roughly 900-500 BC was loose and open to movement; only in the post-Vedic period did birth-fixed rigid caste appear.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy103.txt, section 3.1 Caste in the Past (Portuguese casta, six defining features, Ayyankali box)
question_patterns: distinguish varna from jati in the caste system of India

solution_steps.explain: varna is the broad all-India four-fold classification while jati names the local hierarchy of hundreds of castes and sub-castes
birth-fixation, endogamous marriage, food and food-sharing rules, hierarchy of rank, segmental sub-division, and hereditary occupation together define caste

concepts.title: Principles of the Caste System: Separation, Hierarchy, Purity and Pollution
concepts.section: 3.1 Caste and the Caste System - theoretical principles
concepts.definition: The caste system combines two sets of principles: difference and separation, which keep every caste strictly apart through rules on marriage, food sharing, interaction and occupation, and wholism with hierarchy, under which castes exist only within the societal whole and occupy an ordered rung on a ladder from highest to lowest. This ranking rests on the opposition of purity and pollution - castes nearer the sacred rank high, the ritually polluting rank low - while material power usually tracks social status, and defeated groups were often pushed to low caste status.
concepts.key_idea: Castes are complementary and non-competing - each has a fixed place no other caste may take - so the system works as a social division of labour without mobility.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy103.txt, section 3.1 principles paragraphs (separation, hierarchy, purity-pollution, division of labour, Jotirao Phule box)
question_patterns: what is the role of the ideas of separation and hierarchy in the caste system?
how do purity and pollution decide the ranking of castes?

which scriptural rules were designed to prevent the mixing of castes?

solution_steps.explain: difference-separation keeps castes apart while wholism-hierarchy arranges them on one ladder inside the societal whole
ritual purity near the sacred brings high status, ritual pollution brings low status, and economic or military power generally follows social status

worked_examples.q: Caste ranking rests on the opposition of purity and what?

concepts.title: Colonialism and Caste
concepts.section: 3.1 Caste and the Caste System - Colonialism and Caste
concepts.definition: Colonial rule reshaped caste deeply: British administrators ran methodical surveys of customs, counted castes in the census begun in the 1860s and made ten-yearly from 1881, and the 1901 Census under Herbert Risley recorded the social rank order of castes, provoking hundreds of petitions claiming higher positions. The Government of India Act of 1935 gave legal recognition to scheduled lists of castes and tribes for special state treatment, which is how the labels Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes were born - leading many scholars to call today's caste more a product of colonialism than of ancient tradition.
concepts.key_idea: Once caste identities began to be counted and officially recorded, institutions that had been fluid became rigid - counting changed the thing counted.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy103.txt, Colonialism and Caste (1860s census, ten-yearly from 1881, Risley 1901, Government of India Act 1935, depressed classes, Savitri Bai Phule box)
question_patterns: what changes did colonialism bring about in the caste system?

solution_steps.explain: the census counted castes and recorded rank order, so fluid identities hardened and petitions poured in claiming higher positions
the 1935 Act's scheduled lists gave state recognition to discriminated castes and tribes, fixing the modern vocabulary of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes

worked_examples.q: Under which census officer did the 1901 census record the social rank order of castes: Herbert Risley or Ambedkar?

concepts.title: Counting the Colonial Census Cycles
concepts.definition: The colonial census of caste became a regular ten-yearly exercise from 1881 onwards, and independent India continued the practice; the number of census cycles between two census years follows directly from the span of years divided by the ten-year interval.
concepts.key_idea: Divide the years between the first and last census by the interval to get the count of ten-yearly exercises.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy103.txt, Colonialism and Caste (census begun in the 1860s, regular ten-yearly from 1881; Census Report 2011 mentioned under tribes)

solution_steps.action: subtract the first census year from the last census year
solution_steps.explain: the span shows how many years of census taking separate the two exercises

solution_steps.action: divide the span by the ten-year interval
solution_steps.explain: each interval marks one census cycle, so the quotient counts the exercises

concepts.title: Caste in the Present: Politics, Sanskritisation and the Dominant Caste
concepts.section: 3.1 Caste and the Caste System - Caste in the Present
concepts.definition: Independent India abolished caste in law yet caste stayed central: democratic politics absorbed caste calculus and caste-based parties rose from the 1980s; M.N. Srinivas's concepts name the processes - sanskritisation, where a middle or lower caste raises status by copying the ritual and social practices of a higher caste, and dominant caste, the numerous intermediate castes such as Yadavs, Vokkaligas, Reddys, Marathas, Jats and Patidars who gained landrights through post-Independence land reforms and turned numbers into political power. Caste also turned paradoxical - invisible for privileged upper castes who credit merit, all too visible for scheduled and backward castes whose identity anchors reservations and who still face discrimination; endogamy survived modernisation best of all.
concepts.formula: new_concepts = sanskritisation + dominant_caste ; visibility = invisible_for_upper_caste_elite + visible_for_scheduled_backward_castes
concepts.key_idea: Recruitment in mills, urban neighbourhoods and politics kept organising along caste and kinship lines, while marriage within caste remained largely untouched by change.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy103.txt, Caste in the Present (nationalist movement, reservations, industry recruitment, politics, Srinivas box, dominant caste examples)
question_patterns: in what sense has caste become relatively invisible for the urban upper castes?

solution_steps.explain: sanskritisation lifts status by imitating higher castes, and the dominant caste converts population size plus landrights into rural political power
privileged upper castes experience caste as declining because it secured their advance, while reserved-category members cannot drop an identity that anchors their lifelines

concepts.title: Tribal Communities: Classification by Permanent and Acquired Traits
concepts.definition: Tribe is a modern label for some of the oldest inhabitants of the subcontinent, first defined negatively - no written-scripture religion, no state, no sharp class divisions. Positive classification uses permanent traits (region, language, physical characteristics, ecological habitat) and acquired traits (mode of livelihood and degree of assimilation into Hindu society). By language tribes fall into Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austric and Tibeto-Burman groups; by race into Negrito, Australoid, Mongoloid, Dravidian and Aryan categories.
concepts.formula: permanent_traits = region + language + physical_characteristics + ecological_habitat ; acquired_traits = livelihood + assimilation_into_hindu_society
concepts.key_idea: Tribes range from about seven million members to Andamanese islanders under a hundred, with Gonds, Bhils, Santhals, Oraons, Minas, Bodos and Mundas each a million strong.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy103.txt, section 3.2 Tribal Communities (permanent and acquired traits, language and racial categories, biggest tribes list)

solution_steps.explain: region, language, physical characteristics and ecological habitat are the permanent traits, with middle India holding about 85 per cent of the tribal population

concepts.title: Tribal Population Shares and Census Growth
concepts.definition: Census figures fix the tribal presence in numbers: about 8.2 per cent of India's population, roughly 84 million persons at the 2001 Census, rose to 8.6 per cent, about 104 million persons, in the Census Report 2011; about 85 per cent of tribals live in middle India and over 11 per cent of the remainder in the North-East, where states other than Assam exceed 30 per cent tribal share and some cross 60 per cent.
concepts.key_idea: Multiply India's population by the tribal percentage to recover the census count of about 84 million in 2001 and 104 million in 2011.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy103.txt, section 3.2 Permanent Traits (85 per cent middle India, 8.2 per cent 2001 Census, 8.6 per cent Census Report 2011, North-East concentrations)

concepts.title: Tribal Identity, Development Costs and the Caste-Tribe Debate
concepts.section: 3.2 Tribe - the Career of a Concept / National Development versus Tribal Development
concepts.definition: Scholars first debated whether tribes sit at one end of a continuum with caste-peasant society or differ wholly because they lack purity-pollution ideas, but by the 1970s every standard criterion - size, isolation, religion, livelihood - had failed to hold the distinction, and some now see tribes as secondary products of colonial contact rather than pristine societies. National development, with its large dams, factories and mines sited in mineral-rich forest areas, made tribals pay a disproportionate price through dispossession, deforestation, private property in land and heavy in-migration - Tripura's tribal share halved in a decade - while tribal identities today centre on resistance, statehood wins like Jharkhand and Chattisgarh, and a rising educated middle class asserting culture and resource control.
concepts.formula: development_costs = land_dispossession + forest_loss + in_migration ; identity_bases = resistance + statehood + educated_middle_class
concepts.key_idea: Tribal identities come from interaction with the mainstream, not from primordial traits, and the two great movement issues are control over land and forests and ethnic-cultural identity.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy103.txt, Tribe - the Career of a Concept, National Development versus Tribal Development, Tribal Identity Today, Box 3.1 Xaxa
question_patterns: what evidence would you offer against the view that tribes are primitive communities untouched by civilisation?

solution_steps.action: check the debate and its collapse
solution_steps.explain: continuum versus difference arguments failed on size, isolation, religion and livelihood, so tribes are now often read as secondary phenomena of state contact
dams, mines and forest exploitation dispossessed tribals, and identity assertions today centre on resistance, resources and culture rather than ancient traits

concepts.title: Family and Kinship: Nuclear, Extended and Diverse Forms
concepts.definition: The family is at once a space of warmth and care and a site of conflict and violence; structurally it may be nuclear - one set of parents and their children - or extended, the so-called joint family with more than one couple and often more than two generations, though the joint family was never the dominant Indian form and the very term is a translated, not native, category. Residence rules divide matrilocal from patrilocal societies, inheritance rules divide matrilineal from patrilineal descent, and patriarchal authority contrasts with matriarchy, which remains theoretical since no historical or anthropological evidence finds societies where women dominate - only matrilineal ones where women inherit but do not control property.
concepts.formula: family_structures = nuclear + extended_joint ; rules = matrilocal_vs_patrilocal + matrilineal_vs_patrilineal + patriarchy_vs_matriarchy
concepts.key_idea: Family structure moves with social change - male migration makes women-headed Himalayan villages, and software-industry schedules bring grandparents in as care-givers.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy103.txt, section 3.3 Family and Kinship, Nuclear and Extended Family, The Diverse Forms of the Family (I.P. Desai on joint family)
question_patterns: what are some of the different forms that the family can take?

solution_steps.explain: a nuclear family holds one couple and their children, while an extended family packs several couples and generations; the joint family was never dominant in India
matriarchy has no historical or anthropological evidence; matrilineal societies exist where women inherit from mothers without controlling property or public decisions
